children: By Stefano Rebaudo and Samuel Indyk

German's 10-year government bond yield rose to a 15-year high on Friday as investors remained concerned about persistent inflation and fiscal pressures, while Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh was more transparent on his outlook for rates.
Warsh's comments at the Jackson Hole Symposium had been eagerly awaited but did little to move bond markets in Europe, even if he did provide a bit more clarity on inflation and future rate moves.
The Fed chair said that the central bank would have "work to do" if above-target inflation were to persist.

"Warsh’s speech at the Jackson Hole Symposium delivered a far clearer – and hawkish – message than his last press conference appearance," said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.
His approach to refrain from offering forward guidance on interest rates has unsettled bond markets, helping push bond yields higher, not just in the U.S., but in Germany, France, Japan and others.

"In short, Warsh has now positioned himself much more firmly in the group of centrists on the FOMC, such as Governors Christopher Waller and Lisa Cook, who have indicated that they are prepared to hike absent meaningful near-term progress on inflation," Brown added.
Even so, his comments had little impact on European bonds, with focus on the ongoing impact of the Iran war on inflation, and therefore ECB policy.
German two-year bond yields (DE2YT=RR), which are sensitive to changes in ECB rate expectations, rose 2.5 basis points to 2.873%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Traders were pricing the European Central Bank's deposit rate at 2.80% by March next year, up from the current 2.25%. By late 2027, market pricing implies a roughly 60% probability of an ECB hike to 3%.

Germany's 10-year bond yield (DE10YT=RR) was little changed on the day at 3.25%. It earlier touched a 15-year high at 3.2858%, as bonds have come under pressure this week on worries about fiscal sustainability.
The French spread (DE10FR10=RR) was at 84.5 bps after hitting 86.60 bps on Monday, its highest since November 2024, as France faces a particularly perilous annual budget battle in the coming months.
French growth flatlined in the second quarter, the national statistics agency said on Friday, revising down a preliminary reading and casting doubt on the outlook for the rest of the year.
"Taken together, these figures suggest that the French economy came very close to a technical recession in the first half of the year," Charlotte de Montpellier, senior economist at ING, said.
"This also means that the adjustment required for the 2027 budget will be even greater than previously expected," she added.
